content_review.reason: Вопрос доступен только по видимому stem: что означает стратегия и зачем она нужна. D отвечает на обе части. A классификацию уровней принимает за обоснование достаточности; B приравнивает стратегию к метрикам и превращает долю успешных тестов в вероятность отказа; C подменяет стратегию отчётом и отделяет обоснование будущих проверок. Каждый дистрактор защищаем как распространённое смешение соседних понятий; его буквальная модель остаётся ошибочной без добавления условий.

factual_correctness.reason: CTFL supports the general distinction that planning describes objectives/resources/processes and adheres to policy/strategy; the supplied Q1 theory and correct option D treat strategy as justified selection/prioritization for goals, risks, constraints, and feedback. The exact standalone strategy definition is not prescribed by CTFL §5.1.1, so D is a sound contextual characterization rather than a quoted normative definition.

content_review.reason: A directly defines Chaos Engineering through a controlled hypothesis-based experiment and comparison against a measured baseline. B mistakes a mocked unit test for evidence about a running distributed system; C wrongly says randomness removes the need for a hypothesis; D wrongly equates credibility with maximum blast radius. Each wrong answer is a complete model that can be defended as a plausible misconception without adding hidden conditions.

factual_correctness.reason: Principles of Chaos Engineering (last updated March 2019) defines the practice as system experimentation to build confidence, and specifies measurable steady state, a hypothesis in control and experiment groups, introduced real-world variables, and attempted disproof by comparing steady state. It also directs practitioners to minimize and contain blast radius. These claims support A and refute B, C, and D as written.

content_review.reason: The stem asks for a strategy for choosing test doubles. A answers by selecting a real dependency or double based on the contract, model fidelity, feedback, and maintenance cost. B claims a stub verifies real SQL/database constraints; C treats the count of doubles and verifications as proof of quality; D treats call order as equivalent to the computed result. Each wrong answer is a complete, defensible misconception without invented conditions.

factual_correctness.reason: Fowler’s article distinguishes stubs and mocks by verification style: state verification versus behavior verification. A stub supplies canned answers; a mock verifies expected calls. This supports A’s role-based selection and refutes B and D as equivalences. The theory’s counterexample for B is valid: a stubbed repository can return a value without executing SQL, so it cannot establish SQL or real database constraints. Runtime API behavior was not executed.

sources.used_for: Definition as controlled system experiment; measurable steady state; hypothesis in control and experiment groups; introduce real-world variables; compare outcomes to try to disprove hypothesis; minimize and contain blast radius.
sources.version: Principles of Chaos Engineering, page states last update March 2019

sources.used_for: Mock objects are one form of test double; Fowler distinguishes state verification from behavior verification, and stubs from mocks. This supports separating configured responses from interaction expectations. The local-review counterexample is that a stubbed repository can return canned data without executing SQL; proper real-database verification therefore requires an appropriate real dependency.
sources.version: Article dated 02 January 2007; no separate revision version stated

sources.used_for: Mike Cohn describes unit as the largest/base layer, UI at the top and minimized, and service testing as the middle layer covering application services separately from UI. Supports B’s broad ordering/distribution; it does not establish that all tests must run in that sequence.

§5.1.1: test plan describes objectives, resources, processes and means/schedule, helps meet criteria, and demonstrates adherence to test policy/strategy or explains deviations. §5.1.6: pyramid models differing test granularity and supports automation/effort allocation; layer number/names may differ and high-level tests are generally slower and cover broader functionality. It does not define a standalone strategy document or equate strategy with metric lists/reports.
